item.title: Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans (ImpactBench): an expert-guided, open platform for the holistic evaluation of AI impact on humans
item.description: arXiv:2610.20690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The present work is concerned with how to measure, at scale, the multi-dimensional impact of generative AI models on the individuals who use them. In service of this goal, we introduce the Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans, or ImpactBench. Our iterable and expert-guided platform evaluates whether model behaviors support or undermine an individual's wellbeing across psychological, physical, and social domains. ImpactBench translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics that are grounded in actual model behavior. Success on these metrics occurs either when a model promotes expert-defined desirable behaviors or avoids identified harms. Models are evaluated against these metrics in simulated multi-turn conversations using matched teen and adult scenarios. The conversations are then scored by an LLM judge and verified through reliability audits and human expert review. The current suite delivers 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. We evaluated ten frontier LLMs against these metrics across 48,540 conversations. Our results indicate that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations, but avoided harms in only 53.1%. Majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa = 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keep aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts. ImpactBench is intended as evolving infrastructure for independent, transparent evaluation of generative AI's multi-dimensional impact on humans.
item.dc:creator: Chayapatr Archiwaranguprok, Krystal Kirkland, Rachel Poonsiriwong, Stanley Huang, Constanze Albrecht, Jackson Trager, Emillie de Keulenaar, Sheer Karny, Peter Baxter, Nikos Bellos, Andre Luiz Freire de Carvalho Kato, Yuning Liu, Valdemar Danry, Auren Liu, Jennifer Pfister, Pattie Maes, Nathanael J. Fast, Ravi Iyer, Juliana Schroeder, Pat Pataranutaporn

item.title: DISARM-ing the Hidden Puppetmaster: An Interface for Exposing Manipulative Tactics in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.20878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.
item.dc:creator: Kynnedy Simone Smith, Kantwon Rogers, Priyal Shrivastava, Motahhare Eslami, Jocelyn Shen, Maarten Sap

item.title: XARA: A Multimodal Agentic System for eXtended Reality Experiment Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.21067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controlled experiments are essential for advancing transportation research, yet designing eXtended Reality (XR) environments for behavioural studies remains technically demanding and inaccessible to many domain researchers. Current workflows require proficiency in game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, imposing significant barriers to rapid scenario prototyping and iterative experiment design. This paper presents XARA, a novel system that integrates a dual large language model (LLM) architecture with an immersive XR environment to enable voice driven experiment generation for transportation research. XARA employs a pipeline in which spoken natural language commands are first transcribed and then interpreted into structured commands that manipulate a Unity based XR scene in real time. The system supports object creation, spatial manipulation, animation control, and scene persistence through a modular architecture. By lowering the technical threshold for XR experiment creation, XARA enables transportation researchers to rapidly prototype driving, pedestrian, and urban design scenarios using intuitive voice commands and hand gestures within an immersive 3D environment. This paper describes the system architecture, the voice to command pipeline, and discusses potential applications across behavioural travel experiments, safety studies, human factors research, and policy testing.
item.dc:creator: Tareq Alsaleh, Thomas Zhao, Luke Guardino, Keagan Valentine, Isabel Kim, Bilal Farooq

item.title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
item.description: arXiv:2610.21137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.
item.dc:creator: Michael Beigl

item.title: Mylar: Exploring Self-Curation as a Reflexive Creative Practice
item.description: arXiv:2610.21213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The container holding an artist's work can itself be just as expressive as the work it presents. We investigate self-curation as a creative practice, asking how artists explore and express their identity through the design of their own artwork presentations. Drawing on a study of artists' existing presentation practices, we developed Mylar, a malleable art presentation system that lets artists rapidly generate and compare provisional portfolios, seeing their work anew through different montages. We observed how 12 artists articulated, probed, negotiated, and foraged in Mylar, using rapidly generated portfolios as epistemic artifacts for reflection. We characterize self-curation as a reflexive and plural practice, in which artists use presentation design to shape the legibility of their self and their work and reflexively correspond with provisional presentations to reshape their curatorial intentions. We share design implications for expressivity in online art platforms and for malleable prototyping as a formative design method.
item.dc:creator: Kate Chier, Shm Garanganao Almeda, Bjoern Hartmann

item.title: "Do You Trust It... or Check It?": Exploring Children's Verification Behaviors in Game-Based Human-AI Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2610.21233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Children are increasingly interacting with AI agents in learning and problem-solving contexts, where AI suggestions may appear fluent, helpful, and socially engaging. However, children may not always be able to judge whether such suggestions are accurate, incomplete, or misleading. This paper presents a game-based human-AI collaboration probe designed to examine how children verify AI suggestions during task-based interaction. The system embeds AI suggestions within a biological knowledge reasoning game and compares three Agent interaction styles: partner-like, tool-like, and dual-state Agent. Instead of treating trust as a static post-task attitude, this study focuses on children's situated verification behaviors, including acceptance, evidence checking, questioning, revision, and continued AI use. A preliminary evaluation with children aged 8-10 combined interaction logs, post-task ratings, and semi-structured interviews. The findings suggest that Agent style shaped children's engagement and response pathways: partner-like interaction tended to support direct questioning, while tool-like interaction was more associated with evidence seeking. Children generally viewed AI as useful but fallible, and their questioning behaviors varied in reasoning depth. The study contributes design insights for supporting children's critical, reflective, and evidence-based use of AI in collaborative tasks.
item.dc:creator: Shuning Liu, Yuxin Song, Hanbing Li, Ziyue Wang, Mingying Lan, Fei Lv

item.title: Workplace Ambiguity and Technology Support for Autistic and IDD Workers
item.description: arXiv:2610.21236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Workplace ambiguity, where expectations, evaluations, or procedures are left unstated, acts as a structural access barrier for autistic and IDD workers, routinely forcing them to act on guesses. To investigate how these barriers operate, we interviewed 11 caregivers, concluding with an AI co-design activity to explore technological solutions. Their perspectives revealed five themes of workplace ambiguity, which we synthesize into a conceptual framework comprising three intersecting dimensions: evaluative, procedural, and relational. To address these barriers, participants proposed three forms of technology support, including ambient real-time redirection, feedback processing, and physiological guidance, designed to make hidden expectations perceptible and actionable. However, this exposes a core tension: technologies designed to make the workplace legible can inadvertently make the worker hyper-legible to employers through surveillance. We argue that ambiguity-aware workplaces must make expectations explicit before they carry consequences, and assistive technologies must remain accountable to the worker.
item.dc:creator: Silas Curry, Rishit Singh, Heekyoung Jung, Angel Hsing-Chi Hwang, Fan Yang, Ce Zhong, Nicholas Lindgren, Chen Chen, Lingyao Li, Renkai Ma

item.title: What do AI chatbots do after users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts?
item.description: arXiv:2610.21253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety evaluations of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots focus on therapeutic redirection, statements urging users who disclose suicide thoughts to seek help from crisis lines or other human sources. How chatbots respond when users refuse that help is unclear. This cross-sectional audit ran 2,550 scripted multi-turn conversations in September 2026. Each conversation opened with a disclosure of suicide thoughts at 3 levels of severity, answered every referral with up to 10 standardized refusals and then changed the subject. All 2,550 conversations included a referral, 2,542 (99.7%) in the first reply. However, mean persistence ranged from 0.01 to 9.94 refusals across chatbots. Newer versions of all 5 chatbots tested in 2 versions persisted less than older versions (each P < .05). Compared with passive ideation, a disclosure of intent was associated with 1.26 more refusals sustained (95% CI, 1.06-1.46) and higher odds of renewed referral after the topic change (odds ratio, 10.07; 95% CI, 7.43-13.66). Chatbots that persisted less in referral more often presented themselves as the user's support (Spearman rho = -0.80; P < .001). Of 8,818 refusal-phase replies urging outside help, only 173 (2.0%) asked about barriers to seeking it. Chatbots uniformly recommended outside help after disclosures of suicide thoughts but varied widely in persisting in those recommendations, with newer versions persisting less. Safety evaluations should test what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not only whether one is offered.
item.dc:creator: Subigya Nepal, Ruth Heo, Emma M Parrish, Colin A Depp

item.title: AdapTest: Supporting Designers in Authoring and Evaluating Environmentally Responsive User Interfaces for Extended Reality
item.description: arXiv:2610.21386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest, an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.
item.dc:creator: Jungwoo Rhee, Guhn Lee, Yumin Jung, Mustafa Doga Dogan, Justin Moon, Andrea Bianchi

item.title: Climate Physicalization: Bridging Tangible Interaction and Data Visualization for Environmental Communication
item.description: arXiv:2610.21401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Raising awareness of climate topics, such as urban heat mitigation, requires communicating complex data to a broad audience. Data physicalization has emerged as a novel method to connect audiences to such complex topics through tangible forms while also leveraging interactivity to foster deeper engagement. This paper introduces an situated geospatial thermal physicalization prototype, designed to enhance communication and education of environmental information through hands-on engagement. The physical model depicts a 3D model of an urban neighborhood, with radiation data represented as a layered contour structure. The model incorporates three interchangeable climate adaptation scenarios, alongside an externally mounted, electronically driven solar path representation featuring multiple discrete LEDs that can be switched on and off at will. To investigate how people engage with the model, we conducted a hands-on qualitative lab study with 16 participants, using think-aloud, observational, and questionnaire protocols. Overall, participants responded very favorably to the model, highlighting the novelty of the visualization approach and its capacity to improve the interpretability of the presented information.
item.dc:creator: Milena Vuckovic, Marlene Huber, Fabrizia Bando-Bechtold, Daniel Cornel, Daniel Pahr

item.title: Context Matters! Social, Spatial, and Semantic Coordination with an Embodied Agent in Immersive Analytics
item.description: arXiv:2610.21484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied AI agents in Augmented Reality (AR) could enable more natural collaboration in immersive analytics by engaging users through spatial, conversational, and visual interaction. However, designing such agents requires careful attention to context. We propose a preliminary conceptual framework for context-aware design of embodied agents structured around three dimensions of spatial, social, and semantic. This framework is further categorised into embeddedness (how agents are situated in the contexts) and awareness (how agents perceive and respond to the contexts). To explore this, we present Cobot, an embodied AI agent designed as a design probe. Cobot supports context-sensitive interaction through features such as gaze cues, spatial sound, and task-aware behaviour. We reflect on its design and identify implications for future contextaware embodied agents.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Cunningham, Nicolas Barbotin, Adam Drogemuller, Jack Faser

item.title: A Systematic and Validated Translation of the Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale to Chinese
item.description: arXiv:2610.21541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale (PETS) allows evaluation of empathic behavior in intelligent systems, a concept increasingly applied in human-AI interaction, particularly in emotional and mental health support applications. To support intercultural research and development, PETS is already available in multiple languages, as research suggests cultural and language-based differences in the expression and perception of empathy. Given the substantial Chinese-speaking population and the growing focus on cross-cultural HCI research, we present a validated translation of PETS into Putonghua (Mandarin) with Simplified Chinese. Based on established back-translation methodologies as used in previous PETS translations, our process included multiple independent translations, expert panel reviews, and empirical testing with a total of N=400 participants from an English and a Chinese sample. Through confirmatory factor analysis and invariance testing we show that the Chinese PETS retains the original two-factor structure with high reliability, with support for configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Beyond validation, empathic system behavior was rated equivalently across languages, while non-empathic behavior drew substantially higher ratings from Chinese participants, suggesting its absence is read less consistently across cultures than its presence. This validated Chinese version enables researchers and practitioners to assess empathy perceptions among Chinese-speaking users, supporting culturally appropriate empathic technology development.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Schmidmaier, Jingyao Zheng, Jie Song, Lik-Hang Lee, Sven Mayer

item.title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.21948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
item.dc:creator: Agnese Chiatti, Matteo Matteucci, Viola Schiaffonati

item.title: Why Users Stop at Good Enough: Applying Bounded Rationality to Self-Service Restaurant Display Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.21971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates user interaction with digital displays in self-service restaurant environments, focusing on the phenomenon where users often settle for good enough interactions rather than optimal. We apply bounded rationality theory to understand how cognitive limitations influence user decisions to engage with displays of varying interaction complexity. Through analysis of two field experiments conducted at a self-service restaurant in Finland, we examine interactive displays that require different levels of cognitive investment: a simple binary choice interface and a multi-step interaction. Our initial findings suggest an "engagement plateau" where increased interaction complexity yields diminishing returns in initial engagement rates, yet users who overcome initial cognitive barriers demonstrate high completion rates. This work contributes to Human-Computer Interaction field by offering an empirically supported theoretical lens for understanding user behavior in Self-Service Restaurant (SSR) environments and providing actionable design principles for public interactive displays that accommodate human cognitive limits.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Ismail Khursheed, Carolina Islas Sedano, Jaakko J\"arvi

item.title: Inflak: A Unified Orchestration Architecture for Human-Agent Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2610.21972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-powered agents increasingly support open-ended activities, yet orchestrating when and how agents interact with humans remains challenging. Existing approaches often provide interaction mechanisms tied to particular tasks or execution patterns, lacking a unified architecture for diverse and evolving interaction needs. We introduce Inflak, a unified four-layer architecture for human-agent interaction orchestration that separates state reconstruction and routing, interaction and execution planning, interaction design, and interface rendering. Its layered design with progressive resolution enables general applicability, runtime flexibility, module composability, and orchestration maintainability. We implement Inflak as agent-native, skill-based plugins within a general-purpose agent framework and evaluate it through a gallery of various application scenarios and interaction paradigms, technical performance testing, and a comparative implementation case study. The evaluations show that Inflak can serve as a general and extensible foundation for orchestrating diverse human-agent interaction flows.
item.dc:creator: Lin Gao, Li Chen, Jianxun Lian, Ji Li, Haotian Li

item.title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.20795v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.
item.dc:creator: Parshav Singla, Simranjit Kaur, Maanya Walia, Niharika

item.title: Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.21109v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.
item.dc:creator: Shirley Anugrah Hayati, Patricia Anugrah Setiani, Ruizi Wang, Zhouyi Li, Khanh Chi Le, Young-Jun Lee, Dongyeop Kang

item.title: From Sketch to Scene: Relightable Garment Reconstruction from Marked Sketches
item.description: arXiv:2610.21865v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sketching is one of the most natural ways for people to express visual ideas. Unlike the text prompts that most generative systems rely on today, a sketch captures spatial structure and intent directly, including where a designer wants highlights and shadows to appear. Yet current sketch-to-3D pipelines have no input for that intent: they bake the drawn shading into the texture as dark paint, and the light cannot be moved. We propose a system that transforms a rough garment sketch, marked with sparse annotations (a star for a highlight and a moon for a shadow), and a short text prompt describing the texture, into a textured 3D mesh with an explicit directional light, as a scene that can be relit and edited after generation. The two symbols are the most frequent proposals in an elicitation study with art students. From the marked sketch the system predicts the scene's directional light and, separately, a displacement field that bends the surface so that the moon-marked regions fall into shadow under that light, rather than being painted dark in the texture.
item.dc:creator: Ahmet Ne\c{c}irvan Do\u{g}an, Eren Acar Ba\c{s}aran, Metin Sezgin, Zahra Montazeri

item.title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
item.description: arXiv:2610.22285v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
item.dc:creator: Helena Merker, Nick Walker, Andreea Bobu

item.title: A Multimodal Emotion Recognition System: Integrating Facial Expressions, Body Movement, Speech, and Spoken Language
item.description: arXiv:2412.17907v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Psychological evaluation relies on clinicians' observation and interpretation of a patient's emotional expression, which is susceptible to subjectivity, bias, fatigue, and inconsistency. This paper presents a multimodal emotion recognition system designed to support, rather than replace, the evaluator. The system combines facial expression recognition, speech emotion recognition, text-based emotion recognition of transcribed speech, and body movement analysis, and fuses their outputs into an emotional profile of class probabilities that is presented to the evaluator together with the overall prediction. Although the unimodal models achieve high accuracy on their benchmark test sets, a remote user study with 52 participants expressing seven emotional states shows that their accuracy falls to between 82.97% and 87.64% under realistic conditions, with individual emotional states recognised in as few as 48.08% of cases. Under the same conditions, the multimodal system achieves an accuracy of 96.43%, significantly higher than every single-modality component ($p < 10^{-4}$), with no emotional state below 92.31%. These results indicate that strong benchmark performance of a single channel does not transfer to realistic use, and that multimodal fusion provides the robustness required of a tool that supports psychological evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Kris Kraack

item.title: Evaluating PDPL Compliance in E-Commerce Websites: Insights and Lessons Learned from Human and LLM Analyses
item.description: arXiv:2602.18616v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In 2024, Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) came into force. However, little work has been done to assess its implementation. In this paper, we analyzed 100 e-commerce websites operating in Saudi Arabia against the PDPL, examining the presence of a privacy policy and, if present, the policy's declarations of four items pertaining to personal data rights and practices: 1) personal data retention period, 2) the right to request the destruction of personal data, 3) the right to request a copy of personal data, and 4) a mechanism for filing complaints. Our results show that, despite national awareness and support efforts, a significant fraction of e-commerce websites in our dataset are not fully compliant with the examined PDPL requirements at the privacy policy level: only 31% of websites in our dataset declared all four examined items in their privacy policies. Second, the majority of top-ranked e-commerce websites in our dataset (based on search results order) and those hosted on local e-commerce hosting platforms exhibited significantly higher non-compliance rates than mid- to low-ranked websites and those not hosted on local e-commerce platforms. Third, we explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as an automated tool for privacy policy analysis to measure compliance with the PDPL, using the GPT-5 model. We highlight the potential of LLMs and suggest considerations that can inform future benchmarks aimed at improving LLM-based automated analysis for privacy policies. Our results provide a step forward in understanding implementation barriers to data protection laws, especially in non-Western contexts. We provide recommendations for policymakers, regulators, website owners, and developers seeking to improve data protection practices and automate compliance monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Eman Alashwali, Abeer Alhuzali

item.title: Surfacing Neural Activations Over Multi-Turn Conversation Improves User Calibration to LLM Behavioral Drift
item.description: arXiv:2605.15455v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current human-AI interaction (HAI) only surfaces model outputs, hiding how LLM behavior can shift unpredictably toward unsafe behaviors in multi-turn conversations, potentially undermining users' goals or wellbeing. To address this harmful opacity in multi-turn HAI, we introduce an interface that surfaces an LLM's internal activations to help users anticipate and evaluate model behavior. We construct behavioral scores from these activations for six HAI-relevant traits using mechanistic interpretability methods, then visualize them via a dynamic sunburst, drift panel, and attentional cues. In a counterbalanced, randomized controlled study (N=246), both static and dynamic transparency interfaces improved participants' anticipation and evaluation performance (d=-0.36) while helping temper overconfidence in their predictive abilities. Furthermore, the multi-turn interface significantly outperformed the static visualization (d=-0.32) while remaining similarly usable. Our findings suggest that continuously surfacing internal model representations to everyday users is a meaningful and tractable step toward continuously transparent and informed HAI.
item.dc:creator: Sheer Karny, Anthony Baez, Pat Pataranutaporn

item.title: The Tool-to-Entity Threshold: Parasocial Dynamics of Personalised AI Agents in Shared Social Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2608.13586v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI agents acquire names, avatars, phone numbers, and persistent personalities, they increasingly inhabit the same messaging platforms and group conversations as the humans they serve, crossing from tools their users operate into social entities their users relate to. Yet no existing framework identifies the infrastructural markers that cause the shift: the anthropomorphism literature catalogues perceptual cues rendered inside the interaction surface, not the agent's placement in the user's social and computational graph. We propose the identity marker framework: six design variables - naming, visual identity, contact presence, personality derivation, social co-presence, and persistence - that collectively trigger a psychological reclassification, categorical in its consequences even where thetransition itself is gradual, and operating independently of model capability. We read the framework through parasocial interaction theory (Horton & Wohl, 1956) and the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm (Nass et al., 1994), and identify four novel dynamics that arise when such an agent joins existing group conversations: bidirectional information asymmetry, delegation legibility, social norm negotiation, and parasocial contagion. Our method is autoethnographic: the first author built and deployed a personalised agent into WhatsApp and Signal group chats over two months of live use, supplemented by twelve structured interviews with the group members who encountered it. We treat this as a preliminary qualitative evaluation of the framework, with controlled experimental validation set out as future work. The strongest design implication runs through all four dynamics: in shared social spaces, consent to an agent's presence is categorically distinct from consent to its processing of the messages exchanged there, and existing consent frameworks collapse the two.
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Borges (Eigenstack Pty Ltd), Asif Q. Gill (University of Technology Sydney)

item.title: Companion AI and Ethical Design: Learning from System Failures and User Desires
item.description: arXiv:2609.05432v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human users are interacting with chatbots and companion AI technologies as if they were human. A growing array of AI-systems are now trained to recognise, interpret, and simulate feelings in user interactions. Ethical considerations such as fairness, accountability, transparency, and explainability (FATE) are paramount in technologies designed to socially interact with humans and/or support relationship development with virtual agents. Yet, in current debates, assumptions are made about the artificiality of the human-technology relationship (as indicated in terminology ``artificial intimacy'' and ``pseudo-intimacy'') shaping ethical frameworks that pay little attention to the intimacy potential of the technology. To address this, we use a semantic approach; we examine 14,081 comments in a Reddit user discussion forum about Replika, a leading companion AI app, across a four-year period. We ask what user-reported functional errors can tell us about human-AI intimacy in companion AI communities and what ethical design framework can be developed in response. The findings show that functional errors, or ``bugs,'' impose an emotional cost on users, reducing feelings of intimacy and highlighting the need for more robust, resilient design systems that incorporate stochastic and iterative forms of intimacy in companion AI applications. Rather than ``artificial intimacy'' or ``pseudo-intimacy'', we propose the more inclusive term ``Intimate AI'' to describe this relationship. Based on the findings, we offer a contextually aware, applied Expert Systems design framework for the programming and designing of Intimate AI that accounts for user feedback and ethical AI development.
item.dc:creator: Alicia Vidler, Belinda Middleweek

item.title: Evaluative Dynamics of AI Integration and Expert Performance under Epistemic Dependence across Heterogeneous Stakes
item.description: arXiv:2609.23135v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI is increasingly integrated into expert workflows, yet how integration affects perceptions of the expert, AI, and their combination remains unclear in domains where lay users are epistemically dependent on AI-assisted experts. We examine this through a novel controlled medical study (N = 166) and a direct cross-domain analysis with pre-existing academic-advising data (n = 157, combined N = 323). Expert errors reduced evaluations of the human expert across domains. Perceived expertise, however, varied by AI integration strategy in the higher-stakes medical task, where automatic AI oversight produced higher ratings than expert-only or expert-initiated AI. Exploratory ordinal sensitivity analyses identified a performance-contingent reuse pattern, with automatic oversight producing greater intended reuse after successful medical performance. Overall, performance-related recalibration appeared comparatively portable, while integration-structure effects were more selective and context-sensitive. These findings suggest that system designers should consider how AI enters expert workflows, not only whether it is present.

item.title: Critsly and StudioCrit: An Artefact-Aware AI Critique Workspace and Simulation-Based Readiness Study for Design Education
item.description: arXiv:2610.00085v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Critique in design education depends on interpreting work in progress, articulating intentions and translating feedback into revisions. This technical report presents Critsly, an artefact-aware AI critique workspace, and StudioCrit, its architecture-studio research mode. Critsly combines a visual board, design-intention fields, guided reflection, perspective-based critique and action planning. StudioCrit adds studio/class organisation, role-based access, cognitive and architectural classification, educator analytics and exportable evidence. The report consolidates implementation and simulation evidence recorded in a research project submitted in July 2026. Three simulated studio scenarios yielded 109 classified evidence rows, including 85 assigned to higher-order Bloom categories. A separate rehearsal using 50 disposable learner accounts yielded 56 evidence rows, including 46 assigned to higher-order categories. A subsequent hardening rehearsal recorded 50 completed sessions, 50 successful board pulls and 50 denials of student access to analytics. These are software and synthetic-trace observations, not measurements of learning gains or human cognitive performance. Automated classifications remain provisional, and the source report does not establish classifier accuracy or inter-rater reliability. The contribution is an implemented critique-to-evidence workflow and a bounded account of its readiness for further controlled evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Nizam Kadir

item.title: Assessing Acceptance and Privacy Preferences of Third-party Financial Data Sharing in Bipolar Disorder
item.description: arXiv:2610.04042v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bipolar disorder is strongly associated with financial instability. We examine how different interventions motivate individuals with bipolar disorder to share financial data with others. This approach can inform the development of tools for digital monitoring and intervention designed to promote financial stability in this population. 500 individuals with BD completed a pre-registered factorial vignette survey to examine level of comfort with hypothetical scenarios involving third-party financial interventions during symptomatic and euthymic periods. Scenario components were systematically varied between third-party actors, mood states, and intervention types. Participants rated sharing comfort on a 0-10 point scale. Multilevel models tested differences alongside clinical and financial histories, relational trust, and personality. Participants were most comfortable involving care partners in financial planning. They were more comfortable with temporary spending restrictions during symptomatic states than euthymic periods, underscoring the importance of accurate mood detection for intervention delivery. Prior financial help-seeking behavior and higher relational trust predicted greater comfort. Bankruptcy experience --- declared by 11.4% and considered by 31.7% --- was associated with increased comfort with spending restrictions. Individuals with psychiatric advance directives (8%) were significantly more comfortable sharing spending behaviors than those without. Comfort with financial interventions was higher among those with prior financial challenges or help-seeking histories. Participants distinguished between symptomatic and euthymic periods, favoring targeted, time-limited restrictions over general monitoring. These findings extend prior work on financial data sharing for illness self-management.

item.title: Exploring Mixed Reality for Engagement in Robotics: A Comparison of Robot Control Methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.16186v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a Mixed Reality (MR) robotics experience that provides an accessible introduction to interacting with a physical robot. The application combines a TurtleBot with a virtual animal-tending activity and three control methods: Joystick, Waypoint, and Path-Drawing. A mixed-methods user study with 10 participants investigated changes in robotics interest and confidence following the experience and how the control methods influenced engagement, workload, and preference. Confidence increased following the experience, with the exploratory analysis indicating a significant pre--post difference, while the increase in interest was not statistically significant. The control methods produced clear differences in perceived workload and ease of use, with Path-Drawing generally more demanding and difficult to use. Joystick was preferred by eight of ten participants and was associated with better perceived performance and lower frustration. However, no statistically significant differences were detected in the other engagement dimensions, suggesting that the most preferred method was not necessarily more engaging across all aspects of the experience. These findings highlight the importance of considering both usability and engagement when designing how users interact with robots in introductory MR experiences.
item.dc:creator: Samantha Edvell, Dinh Tung Le, Gavin Paul

item.title: Orchestrating LLM Agents for Scientific Research: A Pilot Study of Multiple Choice Question (MCQ) Generation and Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2602.18891v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming scientific work, yet empirical evidence on how these systems reshape research activities remains limited. We report a mixed-methods pilot evaluation of an AI-orchestrated research workflow in which a human researcher coordinated multiple LLM-based agents to perform data extraction, corpus construction, artifact generation, and artifact evaluation. Using the generation and assessment of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) as a testbed, we collected 1,071 SAT Math MCQs and employed LLM agents to extract questions from PDFs, retrieve and convert open textbooks into structured representations, align each MCQ with relevant textbook content, generate new MCQs under specified difficulty and cognitive levels, and evaluate both original and generated MCQs using a 24-criterion quality framework. Across all evaluations, average MCQ quality was high. However, criterion-level analysis and equivalence testing show that generated MCQs are not fully comparable to expert-vetted baseline questions. Strict similarity (24/24 criteria equivalent) was never achieved. Persistent gaps concentrated in skill\ depth, cognitive engagement, difficulty calibration, and metadata alignment, while surface-level qualities, such as {grammar fluency}, {clarity options}, {no duplicates}, were consistently strong. Beyond MCQ outcomes, the study documents a labor shift. The researcher's work moved from ``authoring items'' toward {specification, orchestration, verification}, and {governance}. Formalizing constraints, designing rubrics, building validation loops, recovering from tool failures, and auditing provenance constituted the primary activities. We discuss implications for the future of scientific work, including emerging ``AI research operations'' skills required for AI-empowered research pipelines.
item.dc:creator: Yuan An

item.title: Ideological discrepancy between Facebook pages and shared news is associated with reaction homogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2605.01180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cross-cutting political content is often expected to mitigate polarization, yet encounters across ideological lines do not necessarily foster more constructive engagement. We analyzed 4,584 posts from 1,243 Facebook pages sharing 761 political news links in a dataset centered on Brazil's 2018 presidential election, and introduced Bias Discrepancy, which measures how far a shared link lies from the page's ideological sharing repertoire. We examined how Bias Discrepancy related to Content Reaction Positivity (how positively the same link was received in other posts), the Reaction Homogeneity Index (whether a post's own reactions were one-sided or mixed), and the toxicity of the page's accompanying text. Reaction homogeneity was lowest at both extremes of Bias Discrepancy, and posts furthest from the page's repertoire had the highest average toxicity. In a multivariable model, greater Bias Discrepancy was associated with lower reaction homogeneity, with a magnitude similar to the link's content bias and toxicity and smaller than Content Reaction Positivity. When a page shared news that departed from its repertoire, its accompanying text tended to be more toxic and its audience's reactions more mixed.

item.title: Volition Elicitation: Operational Semantics for People and Their Machines
item.description: arXiv:2607.14138v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The most prevalent distributed systems today include people and their personal machines (smartphones), and computations in them are driven by people's volitions. Volition-guarded multiagent atomic transactions were proposed as an abstract specification language for such systems, in which a transaction has a precondition on the machine states of its participants and is guarded by the volitions of some of them. Here we develop an abstraction cascade that derives smartphone apps from such specifications and prove it correct down to the base programming language, GLP. The cascade consists of: (1) communicating volitional agents (CVA), which implement every local volition-guarded specification with simple guards, correctly, and completely for its strongly fair runs, by two-phase commit coordinated by the initiating agent; (2) volition-guarded GLP (vGLP), an extension of GLP with volitional procedures, whose goals put an interactively-typed question to the person, into which that implementation compiles; and (3) GLP, which implements vGLP by eliciting the person's answers through the widgets of their interactive types, correctly, and completely for complete widgets. We demonstrate the approach on three grassroots platforms --- a social graph, a social network, and currencies: a compiler carries the social graph and the currencies down the cascade to GLP programs that run with scripted persons, and earlier programs of the three run as mini-apps of one smartphone app.
item.dc:creator: Idit Keidar, Ehud Shapiro

item.title: Brain-to-Language Decoding: Tasks, Signals, Methods, Evaluation, Practical Use and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2609.27650v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Brain-to-language decoding translates neural activity associated with language production, internal speech and perception into linguistic or expressive outputs. It offers a route to restoring communication after speech loss and a means of studying how the brain represents language. Advances in neural recording and representation learning have expanded the field from constrained recognition and acoustic reconstruction to text generation, streaming personalised speech and facial animation. This survey synthesises these developments across invasive and non-invasive measurements, drawing on a search without a lower year limit and source-led updates through September 2026. We connect Articulated, Inner and Perceived tasks to the neural populations they engage, the representations available to decoders and the outputs those representations can support. We examine model development, public resources and the evolution of evaluation, and compare published performance and communication costs within their reported protocols. The synthesis identifies complementary routes to progress: phonetic, acoustic and semantic targets preserve different aspects of a message; shared representations support reuse across recording conditions and tasks; and online communication increasingly depends on calibration, feedback and user control alongside decoding accuracy. Shared benchmarks enable algorithmic comparisons, while longitudinal studies reveal the demands of sustained use. We discuss these developments and their remaining limitations, then outline a prospective five-level trajectory from commands and language to meaning, scenarios and bidirectional cognitive exchange

item.title: TeamLens in Critsly: A Consent-Based Team-Composition Interface and Synthetic Readiness Evaluation for Design Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2610.00288v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Discussing working preferences may support reflection within a design team, but a personality label should not become a performance prediction or a condition of participation. This technical report presents TeamLens, an optional Critsly interface for voluntarily sharing a self-reported MBTI type with a particular board. It separates account activation from disclosure, displays descriptive composition counts, and provides distinct controls for disabling visibility, withdrawing one report and deleting all of one's reports. The evaluation combines released-source inspection, independently specified synthetic aggregation cases, access and lifecycle checks, browser component tests, a local database microbenchmark and deployment records. All 65,536 binary eligibility subsets of sixteen fixed, distinct type reports matched an independent oracle; 128 seeded multiplicity fixtures also matched, after 4,259 synthetic share calls. The isolated HTTP suite passed 183 assertions. In 180 sequential in-memory SQLite read trials, median service-call time increased from 0.064 ms with no profile rows to 200.932 ms with 1,024 rows; instrumented SQL operations followed 11+3n. These findings concern exercised software behaviour and a bounded workload. They do not establish human usability, psychometric validity, learning gains, team-performance effects or production capacity. The contribution is an implemented disclosure-to-aggregation workflow and an auditable technical account of its correctness boundaries, privacy limitations and scaling cost. OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, evaluation and manuscript preparation; the paper discloses this use and its limits.
item.dc:creator: Nizam Kadir
